1.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord, Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed
debates: What the sabbath stands for here
outliers: Ellicott disputes the critical dating that places the writer long after the reign of Hezekiah, and finds an occasion in the closing years of the life of the prophet, against the counsellors of the young Manasseh
Wesley takes the sabbath as put here, like sacrifice elsewhere, for the whole worship of God
Keil and Delitzsch read the beatitude as deliberately extended to those who might think they had no right to console themselves with it
Gill insists that works of righteousness are not to be depended on for justification but are the fruits and evidences of faith and repentance
themes: Jerusalem said never to have fallen had its sabbaths not been profaned
Sabbath sanctity described in terms of clean clothing and emptied occupation
A prophet learning from the books of another when a deliverance would fall due
Blessings said to be as large as the human race

3.pericope_label: Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name
debates: Whether the eunuchs are Israelites or proselytes
What the place and the name promised are
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch decide for eunuchs of Israelitish descent, since the attributive clause used of the foreigner is not repeated in their case
Ellicott knows he stands against most commentators in making the eunuchs a sub-section of the proselytes, doubting that the royal household would have held home-born eunuchs
Ellicott suggests the promise refers primarily to the memorial tablets set up in eastern temples and later synagogues for distinguished benefactors
Clarke notes that the singular pronoun should be read as a plural, as four ancient versions do
themes: A memorial described as an index lifted up to arrest the eye
Ministers told to answer fears they consider unreasonable
Catholicity said to be substituted for rubrics of exclusion
A man calling himself a dry tree, as others called him

6.pericope_label: Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people
debates: What the phrase to serve him covers
Who the outcasts of Israel are
Why the closing oracle carries a solemn formula
outliers: Ellicott rejects the reading that refers the serving to menial offices like those of the temple servants, since the usage of the word limits it to honourable functions
Keil and Delitzsch take the solemn formula as proof that the declaration is not only great but strange and needs confirmation on that account
Gill reads the outcasts as the spiritual Israel whose names men cast out as evil, rather than the captives in Babylon
Wesley cautions that evangelical worship is described here in expressions which suited the worship then in use
themes: A word said to have dropped from the text and supplied from an ancient version
A formula found at the head of a sentence in only one other place
One of a city and two of a family
Worship separated at last from any building

9.pericope_label: His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber
debates: Whether the word rendered sleeping means dreamers or seers
Whether the beasts summoned are literal or figurative
outliers: Clarke reports eleven manuscripts and four editions reading seers against the dreamers of an ancient version, and explains a second variant as a misread letter
Ellicott takes the same pair as deliberate, the prophet with scornful irony substituting dreamers for seers
Gill offers both a literal reading of beasts called to devour the slain and a figurative one of nations comparable to beasts
Ellicott corrects the English to remove an apparent change of figure, the sense being that prophets unfit to be watch-dogs assume the office of shepherds
themes: A dog that will not bark while the beasts come
A letter misread in manuscripts, as the commentator has often seen
Men counting on long years of pleasure and unfurnished for the world to come
Ignorance called most shameful in teachers
